Chapter 1: Setting Out on a Path Shaped by History and Memory
Have you ever felt that odd restlessness you get from reading about journeys taken long ago? Especially when those journeys cut through places touched by both beauty and pain. There’s something magnetic about the idea of retracing a route once walked by a famous novelist—walking through lands that have seen war and hope, side by side.
If you hear the names Sierra Leone and Liberia, what pops into your mind? Maybe images of conflict flash up, but for the people who’ve lived there, or anyone who’s walked those roads, the story is much deeper—much more layered—than headlines can ever tell.
The journey kicks off with this mix of excitement and, honestly, a little unease. The plan? To travel on foot, following the path that a British writer took decades back—a path winding right through the heart of West Africa, starting at the Atlantic coast and pushing deep into the interior. The landscape is lush, impossibly green, but there’s also this heaviness in the air. You can almost feel what’s happened here: civil wars, colonial rule, and the day-to-day fight to rebuild.
Every person you meet along the way—well, they carry their own stories. Stories shaped by survival, by the hope of something better waiting just ahead.
In those early days of the walk, the contrast between past and present is impossible to ignore. You’ll see old colonial buildings, crumbling and worn, their faded grandeur a sort of echo from a time when outsiders tried to shape this place into their own vision. But life doesn’t stop—kids race through the streets, market stalls practically bursting with color, and laughter floats on the wind. It hits you: despite everything, the spirit of this place endures.
There’s something about traveling on foot that makes you feel exposed. Every step reminds you of the distance—not just in miles, but in worlds—between yourself as a visitor, and the people who truly call this land home. You’re always balancing curiosity with caution, wanting to learn but knowing there are things you’ll never fully understand. The road tests you, both physically and emotionally, forcing you to confront your own fears and assumptions.
The memories of war—they linger. You notice burned-out vehicles rusting by the road, and you see scars, not just in the land, but in the faces of survivors. Yet, what stands out even more is resilience. Picture a woman by the roadside, peeling oranges at lightning speed, chatting about her children’s future with such quiet determination. Or a group of young men, huddled around a crackling radio, debating football scores and politics—their laughter a tiny act of rebellion against the hardships they’ve known.
This journey isn’t just about following a line on a map. It’s about really listening—to the land, to the people, to the stories that bubble up from both. Every encounter is a gentle reminder: history isn’t just something buried in the past. It’s alive and breathing right now, shaping every conversation, every step you take.
The road ahead? It’s uncertain. But with each day, that sense of purpose—the reason you started walking in the first place—only grows stronger.
